skill.name: enact-hello-js
skill.description: Run a minimal Node.js greeting example for Enact tool testing and onboarding.
skill.summary: Demonstrates a simple JavaScript command tool that prints a greeting and runtime details.
skill.author: EnactProtocol

security_audit.summary: The reported backtick findings are false positives from JavaScript template literals and Markdown formatting. A separate semantic review found unquoted user input in the Enact command template, which may allow command injection if the runner executes the command through a shell.

remediation.issue: The command template places the name parameter directly into a command string.
remediation.suggestion: Pass user input as a structured argument or ensure the runner quotes and escapes the name parameter safely.

static_findings.snippet: This tool takes an optional `name` parameter and returns a friendly greeting.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 11 uses a JavaScript template literal inside console.log, not Ruby or shell backtick execution. The interpolated value is printed as text and is not executed as a command.
Line 15 uses a JavaScript template literal to print an ISO timestamp. There is no command execution or shell invocation at this location.
Line 16 uses a JavaScript template literal to print process.version. The backticks are JavaScript string syntax and do not execute external commands.
Line 15 is Markdown prose using inline code formatting around the name parameter. It is documentation text and cannot execute commands.
Line 19 starts a Markdown fenced code block for examples. The backticks are documentation delimiters, not an executable shell construct.

semantic_findings.title: Unquoted Command Parameter Interpolation
semantic_findings.description: The skill metadata defines a command that inserts the name input directly into a command string. If the runner evaluates this through a shell without escaping, crafted input could alter the executed command.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The command template visibly interpolates user input without quotes or structured argument syntax. Confidence is medium because the Enact runner may apply escaping outside this file.

content.value_statement: Developers need a minimal tool to test Enact JavaScript execution. This skill returns a greeting with timestamp and Node version details.
actual_capabilities: Accepts an optional name parameter for a personalized greeting.
Prints a default greeting when no name is provided.
Shows the generation timestamp in ISO format.
Displays the active Node.js runtime version.
Demonstrates a small Enact tool backed by a JavaScript file.
limitations: Only produces greeting text and runtime metadata.
Does not validate or normalize the provided name value.
Does not call external services or store output.
Requires a Node.js runtime in the execution environment.

use_cases.title: Verify Tool Execution
use_cases.description: Run a tiny JavaScript skill to confirm that Enact can execute Node.js tools correctly.

use_cases.title: Teach Skill Basics
use_cases.description: Show new contributors how a parameter reaches a JavaScript command and appears in output.

use_cases.title: Check Runtime Context
use_cases.description: Inspect the timestamp and Node.js version returned by a simple tool run.

prompt_templates.title: Run Default Greeting
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill with no name value and show the greeting it returns.

prompt_templates.title: Run Named Greeting
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill with the name Jordan and summarize the greeting and runtime details.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Two Runs
prompt_templates.prompt: Run this skill twice with different names and compare the greeting, timestamp, and Node.js version.

prompt_templates.title: Review Integration Behavior
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to verify parameter passing, default behavior, and runtime metadata in an Enact setup.

output_examples.output: The tool greets World, then reports when the output was generated and which Node.js version ran it.
The tool greets Alice and includes the same timestamp and runtime version details.

output_examples.input: The user asks for a runtime check.
output_examples.output: The response confirms the greeting behavior and includes current execution metadata for troubleshooting.

best_practices: Use simple name values when testing command parameter passing.
Review timestamp and Node.js version output when comparing execution environments.
Escape or structure user parameters before using this pattern in production tools.
anti_patterns: Do not treat this example as a complete production command wrapper.
Do not pass untrusted shell metacharacters as the name value.
Do not expect persistence, network calls, or complex validation from this skill.

faq.question: What does this skill do?
faq.answer: It runs a small Node.js script that prints a greeting, timestamp, and Node.js version.

faq.question: Can I provide a custom name?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill accepts an optional name parameter and uses World when no value is provided.

faq.question: Does it access the network?
faq.answer: No. The scanned files show local greeting output only, with no network request code.

faq.question: Does it write files?
faq.answer: No. The JavaScript file prints to standard output and does not write to the filesystem.

faq.question: Why does it show the Node.js version?
faq.answer: The version output helps users confirm which runtime executed the tool.

faq.question: Is it safe for untrusted input?
faq.answer: Use caution. The command template should escape or structure parameters before accepting untrusted values.
